newsitem.title: USA: Frustrated Dole lashes out at voters, media.
newsitem.headline: Frustrated Dole lashes out at voters, media.

text.p: A frustrated Bob Dole lashed out at voters, the White House and the media on Thursday, appealing to America to "wake up" before it was too late to keep President Bill Clinton from being re-elected.

As his last-gasp effort to persuade billionaire Ross Perot to drop out of the race ended in embarrassing failure, Dole campaigned in Florida, a traditionally Republican state where he is running close to Clinton.
The Republican presidential nominee made no reference to Reform Party candidate Perot during a rally at a junior college here. But, admitting he was frustrated, he seemed to criticise everyone else.

"I wonder sometimes what people are thinking about, or if people are thinking at all, if they've really watched this administration, watched what's happening in the White House," Dole said. "We need to wake America up. It's (election day) 12 days away. Wake up America, you're about to do yourselves an injustice if you vote for Bill Clinton."

The Kansas Republican trails Clinton by double-digit margins in nationwide polls with the Nov. 5 election fast approaching. His sputtering campaign has tried a series of unsuccessful strategies to close the gap.

Dole attacked Clinton and the Democratic Party for taking questionable campaign contributions from foreign interests and a convicted drug dealer and charged Clinton's policies had tarnished America's world standing.
"The truth is he (Clinton) does not reflect the values of the American people. To him this is all a power game. It's a game, it's a game, it's a game," Dole said.

"Nobody respects America any more, we're not feared by our enemies, we're not respected by our allies and our friends," Dole said. "If you want to see this country go down hill in the next four years then you vote for Bill Clinton."

Dole blamed the "liberal media" in part for his poor standing, telling the staunchly Republican crowd reporters were not writing critical stories about Clinton because they wanted to keep him in the White House."The country does not belong to the liberal media, it does not belong to Bill Clinton, it belongs to the people," he said.

Reflecting his campaign's desperation for a breakthrough that could turn the tide, Dole campaign manager Scott Reed went to Dallas on Wednesday to try to persuade Perot to drop his candidacy. But the Reform Party candidate on Thursday labeled Dole's offer "weird and inconsequential."
Speaking in Washington, he said, "Am I in this for the long haul? Yes. Do I intend to campaign to the bitter end? Yes."
Dole refused to answer questions about Perot, joking as he left his hotel for the rally, "If you see Ross Perot tell me."
Perot won 19 percent of the vote in the 1992 presidential election. But many voters have deserted his candidacy this time and he has only around 7 percent in recent polls.

Relations between the two campaigns have been strained, with Dole supporting Perot's exclusion from the recent presidential debates. Still, the Dole campaign calculated that if Perot dropped out some of his supporters might move their allegiance to Dole, making a difference in close states.

Dole is on a six-day campaign swing targeted mainly at the South and Texas. After Florida he went to Montgomery, Alabama, for a crowded rally where he repeated much of his harsh rhetoric. He also goes to Louisiana and Texas on Thursday.

Dole has been trying to shore up his base in the South, a Republican stronghold in recent years. But Dole and Clinton are running dead even in Florida, which has not voted for a Democratic presidential candidate since Jimmy Carter in 1976.
The race is also tight in Texas -- another state that has not seen a Democratic victory for 20 years. Dole has not been in Texas since June.
